Starry rockfish (Sebastes constellatus) attain a maximum adult body length of 46 centimeters [Li = 46 centimeters], placing them among the medium-sized members of the genus Sebastes along the northeastern Pacific continental shelf. This ultimate total length is typically achieved after several decades of slow, sustained growth, a pattern common among long-lived scorpaenids inhabiting cold, deep reef environments. Males and females do not exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism in length, although gravid females in some studies have been found at the upper end of the size distribution. The species is viviparous, and females produce relatively small, yolk-laden oocytes that undergo internal fertilization prior to the release of free-swimming larvae. Prior to parturition, the developing embryos rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves, a strategy that necessitates substantial maternal investment during gestation. Field surveys conducted off the coast of central California indicate that maximum body size may vary locally in response to resource availability and fishing pressure, with individuals from heavily exploited areas rarely approaching the reported upper limit.

Sexual maturation in Starry rockfish begins when individuals reach a total length of approximately 24.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 24.5 centimeters], a size that corresponds to the onset of gonadal development and reproductive competence. Juveniles grow steadily during their first several years of benthic life, gradually accumulating the somatic mass necessary to support the energetic demands of gestation. The length at which half the females in a given population are mature is a key parameter for fisheries management, as it defines the size threshold below which harvesting could impair recruitment. Unlike some congeners that mature at considerably smaller sizes, Sebastes constellatus appears to delay reproductive activity until reaching a moderate body length, a life-history strategy that may buffer against environmental variability by ensuring that only robust individuals contribute to the next generation. Regional variation in the length at maturity has been documented, with fish from cooler, more productive waters maturing at slightly larger sizes compared to those from warmer peripheral habitats. This plasticity reflects the influence of local growth rates on the timing of puberty.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of the species' deep reef habitat, maintained at approximately 12.1 °C [T = 12.1 °C], females release approximately 230,000 larvae per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 230,000 larvae per spawning event] and produce a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = single spawning event each year]. This estimate is derived from the product of average parturition frequency and the number of larvae released per spawning event, reflecting the species' capacity for iteroparous reproduction across a prolonged adult lifespan. The daily rate of larval production is relatively modest compared to many benthic-scattering teleosts, a consequence of the high per-offspring investment associated with viviparity. Gestation proceeds slowly at these temperatures, with embryonic development spanning several months before parturition. The energetic cost of supporting developing embryos is substantial, and females must maintain adequate body condition to sustain repeated reproductive bouts. Studies of captive individuals held at 12.1 °C [T = 12.1 °C] have confirmed that reproductive output remains consistent across successive broods when food is not limiting, suggesting that resource availability, rather than temperature alone, modulates fecundity in this species.

Individual larvae at the moment of parturition weigh approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams], a mass that reflects the small diameter of the fertilized ova from which they develop. This extremely low birth weight is characteristic of rockfishes that produce large numbers of planktonic offspring, each reliant on its endogenous yolk reserves only briefly before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The larval body is translucent and poorly developed at release, lacking functional fins and a fully ossified skeleton, which underscores the vulnerability of this early life stage to predation and starvation. Despite their minute size, the larvae are capable of dispersing over considerable distances via oceanic currents, facilitating gene flow among geographically separated adult populations. The wet weight of the neonate is approximately two orders of magnitude smaller than that of a newly metamorphosed juvenile, indicating the rapid growth that occurs during the first few months of pelagic life. Comparisons with other viviparous scorpaenids suggest that the larval mass of Sebastes constellatus is typical of species that produce moderate clutch sizes relative to maternal body size.

The maximum wet weight recorded for adult Starry rockfish is approximately 1,400 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,400 grams], a value that corresponds to the heaviest individuals sampled in long-term monitoring programs off the coast of southern California. This ultimate wet weight is correlated with the species' asymptotic body length and is achieved only after many years of slow, decelerating growth. In contrast, females at the onset of puberty attain a wet weight of approximately 196 grams [Wwp = approximately 196 grams], representing a nearly sevenfold increase in somatic mass between maturation and maximum size. The dramatic weight gain reflects not only skeletal and muscle growth but also the accumulation of visceral lipid reserves that support gestation. Field-collected gravid females often exceed the average weight for their length class, indicating that body condition plays a critical role in reproductive success. Maximum longevity in Sebastes constellatus has been estimated at 11,680 days [am = 11,680 days] based on otolith increment analysis conducted at 12.1 °C [T = 12.1 °C], rendering this one of the longer-lived species within the genus. This extended lifespan, coupled with delayed maturation and moderate fecundity, defines a slow-paced life history that is highly sensitive to adult mortality from fishing pressure.
